title: "Zebra" sorts before "apple" by default
assumption: Sorting a list of names or words alphabetically puts them in the order a person would expect: apple, then zebra.

input.description: A list of user-entered names, tags, or product titles with inconsistent capitalization, sorted with the language's default string comparison for a dropdown or report.

what_goes_wrong: The default sort returns ["Mango", "Zebra", "apple", "banana"] — every capitalized word sorts before every lowercase word, so "Zebra" ends up before "apple" even though no human alphabetizing this list would ever do that.
why: Python's default string comparison orders characters by Unicode code point and JavaScript's by UTF-16 code unit; for ASCII letters both are the same as byte order. The uppercase letters A-Z (U+0041-U+005A) all come before the lowercase letters a-z (U+0061-U+007A), so a word starting with a capital sorts before every word starting with a lowercase ASCII letter, because the comparison is settled at the first character where the two strings differ and here that is the first letter.
fix: Sort case-insensitively for anything a human will read: key on the lowercased (or casefolded) string, or use a locale-aware comparator (Intl.Collator in JS; Python has no case-insensitive built-in comparator, so pass key=str.casefold to sorted()).

sources.title: Unicode Standard: Code Charts, Basic Latin block
Python docs: Comparisons (str ordering is by code point)

test_cases.note: their_function(a, b) as a display-order "a sorts before b" test should return false: apple belongs before Zebra. Raw `a < b` returns true here, which is the trap.
